Neonatal giant mantas enter the world with a disc width of 192 centimeters [Lb = 192 centimeters], a dimension that permits relatively rapid early locomotion through productive coastal waters. These newborn pups are immediately capable of independent foraging and exhibit a wet weight at birth of 9000 grams [Wwb = 9000 grams], a substantial initial mass that bolsters their chances of survival against predation. The gestation period that precedes parturition lasts for 372 days [ab = 372 days] when measured at a stable water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], a developmental interval that aligns with the slow reproductive tempo characteristic of large-bodied elasmobranchs. This prolonged embryological phase allows for the full development of the large disc and cephalic lobes that define the species, ensuring that neonates are well-proportioned and energetically prepared for the demands of pelagic life from the moment of their first feeding.

The onset of reproductive maturity in Mobula birostris occurs after a considerable juvenile phase. Field observations indicate that first reproduction is deferred until approximately 3285 days after birth [tR = approximately 3285 days after birth], a threshold that reflects the species' late-maturing life history, again recorded under the thermal regime of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. At the point of pubertal transition, females typically possess a disc width of 448 centimeters [Lp = 448 centimeters], a size that signals the achievement of adequate somatic frame to support gestation and parturition. This substantial disc width at puberty underscores the considerable structural investment required before reproductive effort can be initiated, distinguishing this planktivore from smaller, faster-maturing batoids that begin breeding at a fraction of this size.

Females of this species attain truly remarkable dimensions over their extended lifespans. The ultimate disc width recorded for mature individuals reaches 700 centimeters [Li = 700 centimeters], making the giant manta one of the largest living rays. This ultimate disc width is accompanied by an extraordinary ultimate wet weight of 3,000,000 grams [Wwi = 3,000,000 grams] for adult females, a mass that positions them as dominant filter-feeders in oceanic ecosystems. The potential longevity of this species is estimated at 18,250 days [am = 18,250 days] when maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], a lifespan that permits multiple reproductive cycles spanning several decades. This protracted existence allows for repeated investments in large, single pups, a reproductive strategy that contrasts sharply with the production of numerous small offspring seen in many other marine fishes.

Reproductive output in the giant manta is constrained by a low maximum reproductive rate. Females produce a single pup per reproductive event, and births are spaced such that a given female typically achieves 0.3 reproductive events per year [Ri = 0.3 reproductive events per year], as observed under the prevailing conditions of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This maximum reproductive rate reflects a strategy of extreme iteroparity with very low fecundity, where each offspring represents a massive energetic investment. The interval between successive pupping events can extend from two to five years, a pace that renders the species highly vulnerable to population declines from even moderate levels of anthropogenic mortality. This slow replacement rate is a key factor in the conservation concern surrounding the species across its circumtropical range.

Comparative studies with other mobulid rays highlight the extreme life-history strategy of Mobula birostris. The oldest documented individuals exceed 18,250 days [am = 18,250 days], a duration that ranks among the most extended recorded for any elasmobranch, and this extreme longevity is coupled with an age at birth of 372 days [ab = 372 days] that rivals or surpasses gestation periods observed in some cetaceans at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. The disc width at birth of 192 centimeters [Lb = 192 centimeters] is substantially larger than that of smaller congeneric species, illustrating a clear trade-off between neonate size and fecundity. This combination of a very late age at first reproduction, exceptionally low annual fecundity, and a naturally long life creates a demographic profile that is exquisitely sensitive to perturbations, requiring careful management strategies that account for the species' intrinsically low resilience to additional mortality sources.
